title: The Gulf survived a short, hot war. A long, cold one will be harder
author: The Economist
body_markdown:
FOR HALF a century trouble elsewhere was often good for business in the Gulf. The Arab-Israeli war of 1973 and subsequent oil embargo sparked an economic boom in the region. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 brought an influx of foreign capital and a spike in oil prices. This year trouble came to the Gulf itself. Yet in some ways life is returning to normal—as if the trouble were elsewhere entirely.

Flights and hotels are busier. Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), will host a Formula One race and a finance summit in December. In October nine people bought homes in Dubai valued at more than 50m dirhams ($14m), even as Donald Trump threatened to resume a war against Iran that could bring retaliatory missiles and drones raining down on the city once again.

America’s president has retreated from those threats, for now. But danger and disruption remain. In both Washington and the Gulf, many officials expect the conflict to continue throughout 2027, and perhaps until Mr Trump leaves office in January 2029. The Gulf states managed to weather a short, hot war earlier this year. A long, cold one could prove more challenging.

The immediate priority is to keep it cold. None of the six members of the Gulf Co-operation Council (GCC)—Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE—wants Mr Trump to make good on his threats of renewed fighting. “Everyone makes their pitch differently, but everyone starts it with ‘please don’t’,” says a Gulf diplomat in Washington.

But they cannot agree on much else. Qatar is desperate to broker a deal between America and Iran in order to get its liquefied natural gas flowing again. Saudi Arabia and the UAE fear it will be another lopsided agreement that empowers Iran. Instead they are urging America to continue strangling Iran’s economy.

If the status quo prevails, the next two years could look much like the past two months. The Strait of Hormuz would be neither fully open nor shut and uncertainty would linger over the Gulf. Claudio Galimberti, the chief economist for Rystad Energy, a consultancy, expects a “fragile pseudo-normalisation” of the strait next year, in which America and Iran gradually relax their blockades. Others think America will maintain both its blockade of Iranian shipping and its expensive effort to escort friendly tankers through Hormuz.

Either way, that seems good for Gulf producers: they will get some of their crude to market. But, coupled with rising production in the Americas and weak demand, it could mean a supply glut and lower prices—even with the war continuing.

That would be good for the world, but it could prolong the economic pain for Gulf states. In October the IMF projected that five of the six GCC members would contract this year (it revised its forecast for the UAE, from a 3.9% contraction to 0.2% growth, see chart). Only Oman, which sits outside the Strait of Hormuz, is expected to see meaningful growth.

With the war in limbo, expats have returned to the Gulf. Tourists are trickling back, too. But the region has hardly returned to its pre-war normal. Emirates, a state-owned airline in Dubai, carried 22% fewer passengers in the six months through to September than a year earlier. Hotel occupancy is 15-20 percentage points below normal in the city.

A protracted crisis will bring additional concerns. Supply chains are one. Oil may be getting out of the Gulf, but most other commodities, from fertiliser to helium, are stuck inside the strait. Nor is much going in the other direction. Lloyd’s List, a shipping journal, recorded just 227 container ships transiting through Hormuz since March (see chart), an average of less than one per day (the pre-war average was around 20).

While food, medicine and other essentials are still readily available, businesses across the region are struggling with shortages. Bars in Manama, Bahrain’s capital, are running out of beer. A property developer halted a project in Dubai for lack of the right bathroom fittings. Inflation has probably doubled in most Gulf countries this year, largely because shipping goods by road or air costs much more.

A second worry is that a long war will derail long-term investments. The UAE has hoped to make itself a hub for data centres. It has started considering plans to build such facilities underground in order to shield them from Iranian attack. But even if servers can be buried, the infrastructure that powers and cools them cannot. Expats in Doha fear lay-offs and project cancellations if the war continues into 2027. Saudi Arabia is struggling to pay contractors.

Prolonged war will force deep-pocketed Gulf firms and sovereign-wealth funds to spend more on mitigation—from defence to new pipelines and ports—leaving less money for efforts to diversify their economies. Other spending will be cut. Qatar is said to have slashed its foreign-aid budget by up to 85%, potentially a big blow to recipient countries such as Syria.

Governments will borrow to fill the gap. That is a third worry. Allianz, a German insurer, estimates that the Gulf states could run a collective cumulative deficit of $475bn from 2026 to 2030 (3-4% of GDP)—in the previous five years the region’s fiscal balance was close to even.

The pain will not be shared equally. The UAE can balance its budget even with relatively low oil prices and can use pipelines to bypass Hormuz. Having announced its departure from the OPEC cartel in April, it also plans to boost production. “Strait-locked” countries, such as Bahrain, have a higher break-even price and fewer workarounds. They may need help from their wealthier neighbours. But those neighbours will have less to give.

Gulf states find themselves in a curious position: most cannot afford an extended stand-off, yet most are urging Mr Trump to pursue one, because the alternative looks even worse. How long it lasts may depend on America’s new Congress. Some Democratic lawmakers argue that their midterm victory was fuelled by opposition to the war, and that they need to satisfy voters by cutting off funds for it. Others are nervous. “The president would love to be able to say he was on the brink of victory, only for the Democrats to yank it away from him,” says a congressional source.

If Congress does impose restrictions, the devil will be in the details. Halting funds for “offensive operations”, as some lawmakers suggest, could prevent Mr Trump from launching another big wave of air strikes. But it might not stop the blockade or the Hormuz escorts. Nor would it make the Iranians more amenable to a deal. It could just lock in the status quo.

Democrats will also be eager to investigate corruption in the Trump administration. Gulf states invested heavily in the president and his allies. Sources on Capitol Hill expect the UAE to come in for most scrutiny, because of its $500m stake in World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency firm founded by Mr Trump’s family and that of Steve Witkoff, his diplomatic envoy. Qatar gave Mr Trump a jet; Saudi Arabia has done deals with Jared Kushner, his son-in-law. They thought their investments had secured them a firm alliance with a Republican-dominated America. Now they are exasperated with Mr Trump and facing criticism from Democrats.

Iran’s economy is reeling from the blockade, but so are its neighbours. The Gulf states have deeper pockets, though. Many reckon they have no choice but to outlast Iran. The question is how much of their business model survives the wait.
